newsitem.title: EGYPT: U.S. welcomes Russia, EU support for Mideast peace.
newsitem.headline: U.S. welcomes Russia, EU support for Mideast peace.

text.p: The United States envoy to Israel said on Wednesday he welcomed Russian and European support for the Middle East peace process, but that more than one facilitator could complicate the talks, which he saw as close to agreement.

Ambassador Martin Indyk this week joined U.S. special negotiator Dennis Ross, who ended on Tuesday three weeks of mediation between Palestinians and Israelis in a bid to nail down details of the long-delayed Israeli troop pullout from Hebron.

Indyk was speaking at a Wednesday lunch in Cairo where Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said his country would do its best to keep the peace process on the same track Arabs and Israelis agreed at a 1991 Madrid peace conference.
Russia and the European Union are seeking a greater role in helping the talks along.

"The peace process in the Middle East enjoys the support of the international community. Russia, of course, is a co-sponsor of the Madrid process. And France has important interests in the region, and we welcome their supporting role and we welcome a European one," Indyk said.

"We do not have a veto over anybody's involvement nor do we seek to exercise one...But I think that in terms of the negotiations themselves, to have more than one facilitator can immensely complicate the situation," he said.

Israelis and Palestinians return to the bargaining table on Wednesday to try to break the deadlock over Israel's promised redeployment in Hebron, the last West Bank town to be handed over to Palestinian self-rule under the peace deal.

"Yes it's laborious and yes it's taken a long time.." to find an 'implementation mechanism', Indyk said. "But in the process a great deal has been learned about how to meet genuine needs of the other. I believe that we are close to an agreement now."
Israel has said changes of the pullout deal signed by the previous Labour-led government were needed to safeguard the 400 Jews who live and study in Hebron among 100,000 Arabs.
Palestinians want the deal implemented as they signed it.
Indyk said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said that "he will abide by and live up to Israel's international commitments including agreements signed by the previous government."
Indyk said if European and Russian participation was what Israel and Palestinians wanted the U.S. would not oppose it.

Primakov, on a tour of the Middle East including Lebanon, Israel, Syria, Jordan and Palestinian areas intended to boost Russia's role as a co-sponsor of the process, met Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak.

And the EU this week named Spanish diplomat Miguel Angel Moratinos as a special Middle East envoy. An Israeli spokesman expressed satisfaction over the move, and the Palestinians hoped he would help "rescue the faltering peace process".

"We (the U.S.) are in a position to play a facilitating role. We do so at the invitation of the parties, not because we insist on being there but because they want us to be...And when they don't want us to be there we won't," Indyk said.
"And that's why we feel it's better to conduct the negotiations in this way. But it's up to the parties. If they seek some different arrangements then we are not going to oppose it," he said.
